assessment.nobel_worthiness: Z2 topological insulators and the quantum spin Hall effect opened a whole field: topological band theory in time-reversal-invariant systems, protected edge and surface states, and a framework that reshaped condensed-matter physics, materials discovery and spintronics ideas. The concept is original, clear and of lasting generality.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and introduced the Z2 classification; Molenkamp's group gave the first experimental demonstration in HgTe quantum wells after the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. The three-name configuration is reasonable, but the theory credit around Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang and the 3D topological insulator experiments (not credited here) are unresolved allocation questions.
assessment.maturity: Over fifteen years of independent confirmation in HgTe, InAs/GaSb and 3D materials such as Bi2Se3 (ARPES), with stable interpretation. Recognition is timely and arguably overdue, particularly as the 2016 prize recognised the related topological-phase concept.
uncertainties: Whether the prize should cover the 2D quantum spin Hall case and 3D topological insulators together, which may involve other experimentalists and theorists not in the supplied credit.
I am recalling details of priority disputes from memory and have not verified them.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Fluctuation theorems and the Jarzynski equality are exact results that extend thermodynamic reasoning to small, driven, far-from-equilibrium systems, linking the second law to microscopic reversibility. Stochastic thermodynamics now underpins the interpretation of single-molecule, colloidal and nanoscale experiments. It is conceptually deep, original and, as a statistical physicist, I find the clarity of the results compelling.
assessment.attribution: Evans (with Cohen and Searles) gave the early fluctuation theorem; Jarzynski the nonequilibrium work relation; Crooks the detailed fluctuation relation; Seifert the framework of stochastic thermodynamics at the trajectory level. Only three of four credited names may be chosen, and Crooks, as well as Gallavotti and Cohen (not credited), are arguably equally decisive. The configuration is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Validated experimentally in RNA/DNA pulling, colloidal particles in optical traps, electronic and quantum systems over about two decades; theory is mathematically settled. The field is mature, though it is a conceptual rather than a single-discovery prize.
uncertainties: Hard to define a clean, unique discovery and a fair three-person allocation.
Possible perception of bias, since this is close to my own field of stochastic processes; I have tried to weigh it on its merits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution (BB84 and E91) turned the foundations of quantum mechanics, entanglement and the no-cloning principle, into a practical cryptographic concept with provable security. Original, conceptually clear and with large lasting influence on quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard proposed BB84 in 1984; Ekert's 1991 entanglement-based protocol is independent and linked to Bell tests. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is a historical wrinkle outside the credited names. The three credited names support a natural three-person prize.
assessment.maturity: Long-demonstrated in labs, fibre links and satellites, with continuing work on device-independent security; interpretations are stable. Recognition is mature, and the 2022 prize on entanglement experiments leaves a natural complement.
uncertainties: Practical security versus theoretical security (side channels) and limited deployment as a commercial technology.
Credit for Wiesner and others outside the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cold atoms in optical lattices act as clean, tunable quantum simulators of Hubbard-type models. The Jaksch-Zoller proposal and the observation of the superfluid-Mott insulator transition made quantum many-body physics experimentally accessible, with site-resolved quantum gas microscopes extending the reach. The impact on many-body physics is large and clear.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) provided the key theoretical proposal; Greiner and Bloch (in the Hänsch-Bloch lineage) the 2002 Mott transition experiment, with Bloch leading the broader programme. Cirac, Dalibard and others are credited in the list but are less central to this specific discovery in my judgement; the five-name credit must be cut to three, which excludes real contributors and overlaps with the 2001 and 2012 recognitions.
assessment.maturity: More than two decades of independent confirmation across many groups; fully mature, though some of the 'simulation' promise is still being demonstrated and the area overlaps with the earlier BEC and cold-atom prizes.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier cold-atom Nobel Prizes and with trapped-ion and Rydberg simulation candidates.
Unresolved selection among five credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The KTHNY theory of two-dimensional melting, with a defect-mediated two-step transition via a hexatic phase, is a classic of statistical mechanics: renormalisation-group treatment of topological defects giving a new phase of matter. It deeply influenced soft matter, colloids, superfluid films and 2D materials.
assessment.attribution: Kosterlitz and Thouless were recognised in 2016 for the defect-driven transition; Halperin, Nelson and Young completed the melting theory (hexatic phase and its predicted properties). Their credit is clear and a three-person prize is natural, although Kosterlitz and Thouless' earlier recognition makes the extension appear partly derivative to some.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally confirmed in colloidal systems, liquid crystals and simulations, although the order of the transition in some systems remained debated and was resolved only more recently. Mature but arguably not urgent.
uncertainties: Whether the 2016 prize already covers the core ideas.
Controversy about first-order versus continuous melting in some model systems.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry's geometric phase show that gauge potentials and geometry have physical consequences in quantum mechanics. They underlie the quantisation of the Hall conductance, topological band theory and polarisation theory, and appear across optics, molecules and condensed matter. This is a foundational concept with enormous reach.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959) are credited only through Aharonov, since Bohm died in 1992, while Berry (1984) built the geometric phase, with Pancharatnam and others as precursors. A two-person prize is feasible but joins two separate discoveries, and the Aharonov-Anandan generalisation and Simon's holonomy interpretation are unresolved allocation issues.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many experiments (Tonomura's electron holography, interferometry, NMR, optics); fully mature, and its late recognition would be timely only in the sense of being very overdue.
uncertainties: Whether a compound prize can fairly combine two discoveries 25 years apart.
Priority issues (Ehrenberg-Siday, Pancharatnam) outside the supplied credit; unverified from memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened moiré quantum materials, a tunable platform for correlated insulators, superconductivity and topological states. The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the experimental discovery of correlated states and superconductivity opened a very active new field.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key 2011 theoretical prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the 2018 experimental discovery with Cao and others, where early-career co-authors such as Yuan Cao are not credited. The three-name configuration is natural but excludes important experimental contributors.
assessment.maturity: Strong reproducibility across many groups, but mechanisms of superconductivity and correlated phases remain under debate, and the field is still evolving. Recognition may be somewhat premature compared with older candidates.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism and interpretation of the phase diagram are unsettled.
Experimental credit beyond the corresponding author.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical discovery that particles in two dimensions can have fractional exchange statistics is a deep and original idea with consequences for the fractional quantum Hall effect, topological order and topological quantum computation. Its conceptual clarity is high.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) established the configuration-space argument; Wilczek (1982) named anyons and developed the fractional-statistics picture. A three-person theory prize is a natural configuration, with Halperin and Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek for the quantum Hall application outside this entry.
assessment.maturity: Direct experimental evidence of anyonic braiding statistics in fractional quantum Hall interferometers and collider experiments came only around 2020 and is still being replicated, so the maturity is moderate and the timing is arguably slightly early; non-Abelian cases remain unconfirmed.
uncertainties: Independence and robustness of the recent braiding experiments.
Whether a prize should be held until experimental confirmation matures further.
